desc:
Adding features to a browser extension is what Ecom Swift LLC does when you already have a live Chrome or Edge extension and need a new feature or a bug fixed, in the same code style, tested and ready to upload.

## Can you add features to an extension someone else built?

Yes. A developer can add features to a browser extension written by someone else, as long as the code is readable and available. The first step is always reading: how the manifest is set up, how the popup talks to the background worker, where settings are saved and which libraries are in use. Only then is it safe to change anything.

Many owners are stuck in this position. The original developer is gone, the notes are missing and each change feels risky. A careful read-first approach turns that risk into a plan.

## Why careful changes matter more than fast changes

An extension update goes to every user at once, and a broken update can spread quickly through bad reviews. A new feature that quietly asks for extra permissions can also disable the extension for existing users until they approve the change, which causes confusion.

That is why we work in small, tested steps. We check what the old features do before we touch them, then check again afterward. A change that fits the existing structure is easier for the next developer to understand, cheaper to maintain and less likely to cause side effects.

## What a well-handled feature update includes

- A short read-through of your existing code before any edit.
- A written description of the feature or fix, agreed before work starts.
- New code that follows the naming and structure already in your project.
- New settings stored safely, with defaults for existing users.
- A check on whether the change needs new permissions, with a plain explanation.
- Testing in Chrome and Edge on clean and existing profiles.
- A regression pass on the features that were already working.
- A change log written for humans, not machines.
- An updated package and the changed source files.
- Update notes that you can paste into the store's release text.

## How we work through it

You send the code or a link to the store listing, plus a list of what should change. We read the code, ask questions about anything unclear and confirm the plan in writing. Each change is then built, loaded as an unpacked extension and tested by hand.

The packages follow the size of the job. Basic covers one feature or one bug fix. Standard handles a mid-size change with its own screen or panel and saved settings. Premium handles several changes and a tidy-up of the code we touch, so future changes become easier.

We tell you honestly when a request needs a bigger rebuild rather than a patch.

## Do and avoid when changing live code

**Do:**
- Back up the current version before any change.
- Write down what the feature must do in one or two sentences.
- Test the update on a copy before you release it.
- Tell users in the release notes what is new.
- Keep a record of every permission the extension holds.

**Avoid:**
- Bundling many unrelated changes into one release.
- Adding a permission without checking what the store will say.
- Editing the built files instead of the source.
- Skipping the old-feature check after a new feature lands.
- Changing saved data formats without a plan for existing users.

## Who this is for

It suits an owner whose original developer is unavailable. It suits a business that wants a new filter, export button or saved list in its tool. And it suits a developer who is short on time and wants a second person to finish a specific fix.

## What we need from you

Send the extension source as a zip or repository invite, or the store link if the code is on its way. Describe what should change, who it is for and any screens you have in mind.

We never ask for passwords. If you want the new version published, we explain the steps, or you can add us to your store account with the limited access it offers. After you order, we reply with questions and a short plan before we begin.
